title: Subtree of Another Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: `isSubtree(root, subRoot)` checks whether `subRoot` is structurally and value-identical to any subtree of `root`.
Idea: Compare the trees with nested `same(a, b)`, then try each node of `root` as a candidate root.
Technique and why it applies: `same` checks matching null structure, equal `val` fields, and both child pairs; `self.isSubtree` recursively searches `root.left` and `root.right` if the current root does not match.
Invariant: Each recursive search returns true exactly when a candidate subtree rooted at that node matches `subRoot`.
Edge cases: A null `subRoot` returns true; a nonempty `subRoot` cannot match a null `root`; equal values alone are insufficient without matching shape.
Complexity: O(nm) worst-case time for n nodes in `root` and m in `subRoot`; O(h+h2) recursion space for the two tree heights.
complexity_reason: The same-tree helper checks both values and child structure, so repeated candidate comparisons may inspect up to m nodes each.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: `isSubtree(TreeNode root, TreeNode subRoot)` checks whether `subRoot` occurs as an identical rooted subtree of `root`.
Idea: Treat a null `subRoot` as a match, reject a null `root`, and otherwise test the current node before searching both children.
Technique and why it applies: `same(TreeNode a, TreeNode b)` compares null positions, `val`, `left`, and `right`; recursive `isSubtree` calls enumerate all possible candidate roots.
Invariant: `same` returns true only for equal tree shape and values, and `isSubtree` succeeds if any candidate root passes that test.
Edge cases: Empty `subRoot` returns true; a nonempty target with null `root` returns false; equal root values do not suffice if descendants differ.
Complexity: O(nm) worst-case time and O(h+h2) recursive stack space for tree heights h and h2.
complexity_reason: Each candidate can trigger a full `same` traversal of the target tree, giving the O(nm) worst case.

title: Distribute Candies
notes:
Task and constraints: `distributeCandies(candyType)` finds the maximum number of distinct types among the half of an even-sized candy array assigned to the sister.
Idea: Return the smaller of the number of distinct types and half the candy count.
Technique and why it applies: `len(set(candyType))` counts available types, while `len(candyType)//2` caps how many candies she can receive.
Invariant: The answer cannot exceed either available distinct types or the number of candies allocated, and both limits are achievable by choosing distinct types first.
Edge cases: Repeated candy labels reduce the distinct-type bound; when every candy has a unique type, the half-array bound controls the answer.
Complexity: O(n) expected time to build the set and O(n) space for distinct types.
code:
class Solution:
 def distributeCandies(self,candyType): return min(len(set(candyType)),len(candyType)//2)
complexity_reason: The sister can take at most one candy of each type and cannot receive more than half of all candies.

title: Distribute Candies
notes:
Task and constraints: `distributeCandies(int[] candyType)` returns the greatest possible number of distinct types in a selection of exactly half the even-length array.
Idea: Collect types in a `HashSet<Integer>` and take the minimum of its size and `candyType.length / 2`.
Technique and why it applies: `s.add(x)` deduplicates candy types; `Math.min` applies the distinct-type limit and the allocation-size limit.
Invariant: Every distinct type can contribute at most one to the count, and the sister cannot select more candies than the half-array allocation.
Edge cases: All duplicate types yield one distinct type; all unique types cap the result at half the array length.
Complexity: O(n) expected time for hash-set insertion and O(n) auxiliary space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int distributeCandies(int[] candyType){Set<Integer>s=new HashSet<>();for(int x:candyType)s.add(x);return Math.min(s.size(),candyType.length/2);} }
complexity_reason: The set counts each type once, while integer division gives the exact number of candies assigned to the sister.

title: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
notes:
Task and constraints: `findUnsortedSubarray(nums)` returns the shortest contiguous interval that must be sorted to make the whole array nondecreasing.
Idea: Find the first left and right disorder boundaries, calculate the interval's minimum and maximum, then extend boundaries to include out-of-place neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: The initial `while` loops skip already sorted prefixes and suffixes; `min(nums[l:r+1])` and `max(...)` identify values that may need to cross the interval edges.
Invariant: After extension, no element immediately outside `[l, r]` violates sorted order relative to the interval's minimum or maximum.
Edge cases: Already sorted input returns zero; duplicates are handled by the `<=` comparisons; the method assumes a list of ordinary comparable numbers.
Complexity: O(n) time across a constant number of scans and O(1) auxiliary space.
code:
class Solution:
 def findUnsortedSubarray(self,nums):
  n=len(nums);l=0
  while l<n-1 and nums[l]<=nums[l+1]:l+=1
  if l==n-1:return 0
  r=n-1
  while r>0 and nums[r-1]<=nums[r]:r-=1
  lo,hi=min(nums[l:r+1]),max(nums[l:r+1])
  while l>0 and nums[l-1]>lo:l-=1
  while r<n-1 and nums[r+1]<hi:r+=1
  return r-l+1
complexity_reason: The interval's minimum and maximum reveal whether the preceding or following sorted elements must be included.

title: Shortest Unsorted Continuous Subarray
notes:
Task and constraints: `findUnsortedSubarray(int[] a)` computes the length of the smallest interval whose sorting orders the full array.
Idea: Skip the sorted prefix and suffix, find `lo` and `hi` inside the disorder region, and extend `l` and `r` while neighboring values violate those bounds.
Technique and why it applies: The scan computes `Integer.MAX_VALUE`/`Integer.MIN_VALUE` bounds using `Math.min` and `Math.max`; `a[l-1] > lo` and `a[r+1] < hi` detect elements that belong inside the interval.
Invariant: The final interval contains every value that must move across its boundaries to restore global order.
Edge cases: A fully sorted array returns zero; `l` and `r` checks prevent out-of-bounds access; equal adjacent values remain valid.
Complexity: O(n) time over several linear scans and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The extension loops include any outside value that would violate the sorted order after the interior is sorted.

title: Delete Operation for Two Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: `minDistance(word1, word2)` finds the minimum deletions needed to make two strings equal while preserving the order of remaining characters.
Idea: Compute the longest common subsequence with a one-dimensional DP array, then subtract twice its length from the combined string lengths.
Technique and why it applies: `dp[j]` represents the LCS length for the processed prefix of `word1` and first `j` characters of `word2`; `diagonal` preserves the old upper-left state as each cell is updated.
Invariant: After each outer iteration, `dp[j]` is the LCS length for the processed prefix of `word1` and `word2[:j]`.
Edge cases: Either empty string gives the other string's length as deletions; equal characters extend the diagonal LCS state.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(n) auxiliary space for string lengths m and n.
complexity_reason: Only characters in the LCS can remain in both strings, so every other character must be deleted from one side.

title: Delete Operation for Two Strings
notes:
Task and constraints: `minDistance(String a, String b)` returns the minimum deletions needed to make both strings equal.
Idea: Use a one-dimensional `dp` array to calculate the longest common subsequence, then return `a.length() + b.length() - 2 * dp[b.length()]`.
Technique and why it applies: `diagonal` stores the previous row's diagonal value, `old` preserves `dp[j]`, and `Math.max(dp[j], dp[j-1])` selects the best subsequence when characters differ.
Invariant: After processing each character of `a`, `dp[j]` represents the LCS length for the processed prefix and `b.substring(0, j)`.
Edge cases: Empty strings are handled by the zero-initialized array; identical strings require zero deletions.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(n) auxiliary space, where m and n are the input lengths.
complexity_reason: The common subsequence is retained in both strings, requiring deletion of all other characters from the combined lengths.

title: N-ary Tree Preorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: `preorder(root)` returns an N-ary tree traversal that visits each node before its children, from left to right.
Idea: Build `out` and use nested recursive `dfs(n)` to append each node before visiting its children.
Technique and why it applies: `out.append(n.val)` happens before the `for c in n.children` loop, which establishes preorder; the null check stops recursion for an absent node.
Invariant: Whenever a node is appended, its value appears before every descendant in the output, and child subtrees are traversed in listed order.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty list; a leaf contributes only its value.
Complexity: O(n) time visits each node once and O(h) recursion space excluding the O(n) output list.
complexity_reason: Appending `n.val` before recursively visiting `n.children` is the defining root-first preorder order.

title: N-ary Tree Preorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: `preorder(Node root)` returns node values in root-first, left-to-right N-ary tree order.
Idea: Initialize `out`, then let `dfs` append a node before recursively processing each child.
Technique and why it applies: `out.add(n.val)` precedes `for (Node c : n.children) dfs(c, out)`, so each parent's value appears before all descendants.
Invariant: The output contains every visited node once, with each node before its descendants and sibling subtrees in child-list order.
Edge cases: A null root is ignored by `dfs` and yields an empty list; a leaf adds one value.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursive stack space excluding the output list.
complexity_reason: The helper returns immediately on null and appends a node before iterating through its children.

title: N-ary Tree Postorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: `postorder(root)` returns an N-ary tree traversal with each node visited after all its children, processing children left to right.
Idea: Use `dfs(n)` to recurse through `n.children` before appending `n.val` to `out`.
Technique and why it applies: The placement of `out.append(n.val)` after the child loop guarantees that all descendants are emitted before their parent.
Invariant: A node is appended only after every child subtree has completed, while the order of sibling subtrees follows `n.children`.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty list; a leaf is appended immediately because its child loop is empty.
Complexity: O(n) time visits each node once and O(h) recursion space excluding the output list.
complexity_reason: Placing `out.append(n.val)` after the child loop makes the traversal child-first and root-last.

title: N-ary Tree Postorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: `postorder(Node root)` emits an N-ary tree's values after visiting each node's children from left to right.
Idea: Build the result list and use `dfs` to traverse children before adding the current node.
Technique and why it applies: `for (Node c : n.children) dfs(c, out)` completes all child subtrees before `out.add(n.val)` executes.
Invariant: Each node enters the result after all its descendants, and siblings appear in the order stored in `children`.
Edge cases: A null root returns an empty list; a leaf has no child calls and is appended directly.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursive stack space excluding the output list.
complexity_reason: The recursive calls finish the child subtrees before the current node is added to `out`.

title: Longest Harmonious Subsequence
notes:
Task and constraints: `findLHS(nums)` returns the longest subsequence length whose maximum and minimum differ by exactly one.
Idea: Count each value with `Counter`, then test adjacent values `x` and `x + 1` and maximize their combined frequencies.
Technique and why it applies: `f[x] + f[x+1]` uses every occurrence of two neighboring values, and `x+1 in f` ensures the difference is exactly one.
Invariant: Each candidate count represents a valid harmonious subsequence containing all occurrences of those two values.
Edge cases: If no neighboring values occur, `default=0` returns zero; repeated values alone do not form a harmonious subsequence.
Complexity: O(n) expected time to count and inspect values, and O(n) space for the frequency map.
complexity_reason: A valid harmonious subsequence must use two present values differing by exactly one, so their frequencies can be summed.

title: Longest Harmonious Subsequence
notes:
Task and constraints: `findLHS(int[] nums)` finds the largest subsequence whose maximum and minimum values differ by one.
Idea: Count values in `Map<Integer, Integer> f`, then compare each key with its successor when that successor exists.
Technique and why it applies: `f.containsKey(x + 1)` confirms the required adjacent value, and `Math.max` updates `best` with `f.get(x) + f.get(x + 1)`.
Invariant: `best` is the greatest combined frequency among all neighboring value pairs examined so far.
Edge cases: No adjacent values produces zero; duplicates are counted through frequency increments; integer-boundary inputs should respect the problem's value constraints for `x + 1`.
Complexity: O(n) expected time for hash-map counting and lookup, and O(n) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The algorithm sums frequencies only for pairs whose values differ by exactly one, excluding single-value groups.

title: Range Addition II
notes:
Task and constraints: `maxCount(m, n, ops)` counts cells with the maximum value after each operation increments a top-left rectangle in an initially zero matrix.
Idea: Find the minimum row extent and column extent across all operations and multiply them.
Technique and why it applies: `min((a for a, _ in ops), default=m)` and the corresponding column expression compute the common intersection of every incremented rectangle; cells in that intersection receive every operation.
Invariant: The intersection dimensions are the smallest operation bounds, and exactly those cells achieve the maximum number of increments.
Edge cases: With no operations, the default dimensions return `m * n`; narrow operations reduce one or both dimensions.
Complexity: O(q) time for q operations and O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the input.
complexity_reason: The cells inside every operation's shared top-left intersection receive all increments and therefore have maximum value.

title: Range Addition II
notes:
Task and constraints: `maxCount(int m, int n, int[][] ops)` counts maximum-valued cells after top-left rectangle increments.
Idea: Start `rows` and `cols` at the full dimensions and reduce each to the minimum bounds in `ops`.
Technique and why it applies: `Math.min(rows, op[0])` and `Math.min(cols, op[1])` find the intersection shared by every increment operation; `rows * cols` counts its cells.
Invariant: After each operation, `rows` and `cols` describe the common prefix rectangle covered by all operations processed so far.
Edge cases: An empty `ops` array leaves the full matrix dimensions, so every cell is maximal; smaller operation bounds shrink the intersection.
Complexity: O(q) time over q operations and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Every operation increments its top-left rectangle, so only cells in the intersection receive every increment.

title: Minimum Index Sum of Two Lists
notes:
Task and constraints: `findRestaurant(list1, list2)` returns all common strings with the smallest sum of their indices in the two lists.
Idea: Map each string in `list1` to its index, then scan `list2` and track the minimum sum in `best`.
Technique and why it applies: `idx[s] + j` computes the index sum; a lower value resets `out`, while an equal value appends another valid tie.
Invariant: After each common string is processed, `best` is the smallest sum seen and `out` contains exactly the strings attaining it.
Edge cases: No common strings leaves the result empty; multiple strings can tie for the minimum; this approach assumes each list has unique restaurant names for single-index lookup.
Complexity: O(m+n) expected time and O(m) auxiliary space for the index map.
complexity_reason: Resetting `out` on a strictly smaller index sum preserves ties only for the current minimum.

title: Minimum Index Sum of Two Lists
notes:
Task and constraints: `findRestaurant(String[] a, String[] b)` returns all common strings whose indices sum to the minimum.
Idea: Store indices from `a` in `idx`, scan `b`, and update `best` and `out` for each common string.
Technique and why it applies: `idx.get(b[j])` finds the first-list index; a smaller `v` clears `out`, while `v == best` preserves all minimum-sum ties.
Invariant: `best` is the lowest index sum observed among common strings, and `out` contains exactly those strings seen with that sum.
Edge cases: No overlap returns an empty array; tied minima are all included; the standard problem assumes unique strings in each list.
Complexity: O(m+n) expected time and O(m) auxiliary space for the hash map and result list.
complexity_reason: Clearing the result list only when a strictly smaller sum appears retains every string tied at the current minimum.

title: Can Place Flowers
notes:
Task and constraints: `canPlaceFlowers(flowerbed, n)` determines whether `n` flowers can be planted without adjacent occupied plots.
Idea: Return true for nonpositive `n`; otherwise scan left to right and plant at every empty plot whose neighbors are empty or outside the array.
Technique and why it applies: The conditions `i == 0`, `i == len(flowerbed)-1`, and neighboring zero checks guard boundaries; marking `flowerbed[i] = 1` prevents planting beside a newly planted flower.
Invariant: Before each position is considered, all earlier new flowers are separated from each other and from existing flowers by at least one plot.
Edge cases: `n <= 0` succeeds immediately; an empty bed with positive `n` fails; the method mutates the input list and may return early once enough flowers are planted.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Greedily planting at the earliest valid empty plot leaves the largest available space for later placements.

title: Can Place Flowers
notes:
Task and constraints: `canPlaceFlowers(int[] bed, int n)` checks whether the flowerbed can accept `n` flowers without adjacent plantings.
Idea: Handle `n <= 0`, then scan for empty plots whose left and right neighbors are also empty or beyond the array.
Technique and why it applies: The boundary checks `i == 0` and `i == bed.length - 1` prevent invalid neighbor access; `bed[i] = 1` blocks adjacent future placements and `++planted` counts additions.
Invariant: Each newly planted flower is separated from existing and newly planted flowers by at least one empty plot.
Edge cases: Nonpositive `n` returns true; an empty bed with positive `n` returns false; the input array is modified and the method can exit early.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The earliest valid placement is safe because it occupies no plot adjacent to an existing flower and preserves later options.
